newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Stress, the health hazard of modern life.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Stress, the health hazard of modern life.

text.p: On a scale of stress from one to 100, the death of a spouse scores the maximum points and divorce 73. Holidays and Christmas also score double-digit figures.
Recognised as the health hazard of modern life, stress can contribute, directly or indirectly, to heart disease, cancer and strokes, as well as a host of psychological problems.
Children are as likely to suffer from it as adults. No one, regardless of how calm their personality, is immune.
"It is not only a yuppie problem," said Mark Greener, author of a new book called "Managing Stress".

"In fact, it is often people who have little or no control over certain aspects of their lives -- such as those in routine jobs or the unemployed -- who suffer particularly badly," added Greener, a pharmacologist and medical journalist.
Up to half of sickness absence is due to work-related stress and depression, costing an estimated seven billion pounds ($11 billion) in lost revenue in Britain alone each year.

Most people can cope with, and even need a certain amount of stress to perform to the peak of their ability. But when demands for dealing with stress outstrip resources, strength or time it becomes dangerous.
"Stress is a response to change in the environment. Anything that leads to change can cause stress, even if it's enjoyable," explained Greener.

Britain's Trade Union Congress, concerned after a survey of workers revealed that stress was the biggest health hazard they faced, have launched a nationwide campaign to combat what it called the "new industrial epidemic."
Stress has even become a political issue. The opposition Labour Party, strongly tipped to win the next general election, has vowed to reduce workplace stress.
"Working long hours is a major cause of stress, (along) with bullying in the workplace," said its health spokesman Graham Allen.

Stress is not a new problem. It has existed since cavemen foraged for food and hunted wild animals. But people are a lot better now at recognising it and there is an increasing awareness among doctors that it contributes to a wide range of diseases.

Many believed the computer age and the sexual revolution would improve lifestyles and give men and women more free time, But Greener says people are now working longer hours, have more information to cope with and are feeling more insecure.
"There is a great deal of uncertainty in the workplace. The old thing of having a job for life is gone," he said.

"People's roles are also in transition. The traditional role of women has changed and that creates conflicts between their role as mother and wife and their role in the workplace. We are going through a transition."
Greener attributes juggling the demands of home, children and jobs, plus the prejudice they face in the workplace, as the main causes of stress for women.
"For men it is the changing (sexual) roles and the lack of security they tend to rely on," he explained.
Even young children are not immune from stress. The patterns of adult strategies for coping with stress are developed in childhood, Greener said.

Managers are also complaining of being stressed by information overload. A recent poll of 1,313 executives in Singapore, the United States, Hong Kong, Britain and Australia found substantial numbers suffering from an information glut.
"Having too much information can be as dangerous as having too little," said psychologist David Lewis who analysed the survey results.
"What this report makes crystal clear is that finding ways of dealing with the information burden is now one of the most urgent world-wide challenges facing business."
Studies have confirmed that certain personality types are better at coping with stress.
Type A personalities who are very competitive, impatient, aggressive and restless tend to suffer while the unhurried, relaxed and more passive B types don't.

Headaches, anxiety, panic attacks, sweating, twitching and fear are among the most common symptoms of stress but Greener emphasised that the manifestations are as individual as the triggers and the techniques for dealing with it.

What is important is for people to recognise what causes them to feel stressed and then to find the most effective way to relieve it, be it yoga, sports, psychotherapy or a variety of holistic therapies.
"The one strain that comes out of every single stress technique is that it forces people to take time out for themselves and that is the key," said Greener.
"Everyone is stressed. It is a fact of life," he added. "What we have to do is to try to manage it."
